title: Cutting off dead ends
objectives: Prune a backtracking search to make it fast enough.
Solve N-queens and subset sum with pruning
Tell a safe prune from one that loses answers

screens.title: Four queens
screens.prose: We want four queens on a 4 by 4 board, none attacking another. A queen attacks along its row, its column and both diagonals. One queen sits in row 1.
screens.question: Tap every cell in rows 2 to 4 where a second queen would be safe from it.

hints.text: Rule out the queen's column first, then its two diagonals.
These cells sit on the queen's diagonals.
Column 2 is attacked, and so are r2c1, r2c3 and r3c4 on the diagonals. The other six cells are safe.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A cell is attacked if it shares the queen's column or a diagonal.

byKey.no-diag: You ruled out the column but not the diagonals. A queen also attacks corner to corner.
byKey.r2c1: r2c1 is one step down and left of the queen: on its diagonal.
byKey.r2c3: r2c3 is one step down and right of the queen: on its diagonal.
byKey.r3c4: r3c4 is two steps down and two right: on the queen's diagonal.
byKey.r3c2: Column 2 holds the queen, so every cell below it is attacked.

explain.text: Column 2 and the diagonals through r1c2 are attacked. Six cells survive. A search that only ever places a queen on a safe cell never wastes time on the rest.

screens.title: One queen per row
screens.prose: The search places one queen per row, top to bottom. Row 2 had one safe cell, r2c4, so a queen went there. Tap cells to test them.
screens.question: Tap every cell in rows 3 and 4 that neither queen attacks.

hints.text: Columns 2 and 4 are gone. Check the diagonals of both queens.
r2c4 attacks this cell diagonally.
Row 3 keeps only r3c1. Row 4 keeps r4c1 and r4c3.

feedback.correct: r3c1 in row 3, and r4c1 and r4c3 in row 4.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each cell against both queens.

byKey.r3c3: r3c3 is one step down and left of the queen on r2c4: a diagonal.

explain.text: Row 3 has one safe cell, r3c1. Once a queen sits there, it attacks r4c1, which leaves r4c3. Four queens fit: r1c2, r2c4, r3c1, r4c3.

screens.title: All the answers
screens.prose: The search tries every column in row 1. Whenever a row has no safe cell left, it is a dead end: the search steps back and moves the queen above.
screens.question: How many different ways are there to place the four queens safely?

widget.label: Number of placements
widget.accept: 2: this one and its mirror image.

hints.text: Try each column for the row 1 queen and follow the safe cells.
A queen in a corner of row 1 leads to a dead end by row 3.
From r1c2 there is this answer; from r1c3 there is its mirror image. Corners fail.

feedback.correct: Two placements, mirror images of each other.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Try the row 1 queen in each of the four columns.

byKey.one: You found the answer above. Its mirror image, starting from r1c3, works too.
byKey.rows: You counted one per row 1 column. Starting in a corner runs into a dead end.
byKey.orders: You counted $4!$ column orders. Most of those put queens on a shared diagonal.

explain.text: Starting from r1c1 or r1c4, row 3 or row 4 runs out of safe cells. Cutting off a branch as soon as it cannot lead to an answer is called **pruning**. Exactly two placements survive.

screens.title: What pruning saves
screens.prose: Without pruning, the search puts a queen in any column of each row and checks only at the end. With pruning, it only steps onto safe cells. Count the partial boards each one visits.

state.caption: From r1c1, row 2 has 2 safe cells

screens.question: Fill in the boards visited at each depth.

hints.text: Without pruning each board has 4 children. With pruning, count the safe row 2 cells under each row 1 column.
From r1c1 there are 2 safe cells in row 2.
Safe row 2 cells under columns 1 to 4: 2, 1, 1, 2, so 6. Full boards with pruning are the answers: 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each depth in turn.

byKey.r2c1: Without pruning every board branches 4 ways: $4 \times 4 = 16$.
byKey.r2c2: Under each row 1 column, count the safe cells in row 2: $2 + 1 + 1 + 2$.
byKey.r4c2: Full boards reached with pruning are exactly the answers.

explain.text: Without pruning the search visits $1 + 4 + 16 + 64 + 256 = 341$ boards; with pruning, 17. For 8 queens it is 19,173,961 against 2,057. Pruning does not change the answers, only the work.

screens.title: Subsets that hit a target
screens.prose: Now find every subset of the positive numbers 3, 5 and 6 that sums to exactly 8. The walk keeps a running total and refuses any *take* that would push it past 8.
screens.question: Tap every *take 6* branch the walk refuses.

hints.text: Before each *take 6*, look at the running total so far.
Here the total is already 8 before the 6.
A take of 6 fits only when the total so far is at most 2. That is only true when 3 and 5 were both skipped.

feedback.correct: Three branches are cut; one subset, 3 + 5, hits 8.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add 6 to the total before each branch and compare with 8.

byKey.n-n-y: Here 3 and 5 were both skipped, so the total is 0 and 6 fits. It ends at 6, not 8, but nothing pushed it past 8.

explain.text: The three cut branches would reach 14, 9 and 11. With only positive numbers a total can never come back down, so nothing below a cut branch could hit 8. The one answer is 3 + 5.

canvas.caption: Cut branches in blue; the answer 3 + 5 highlighted

screens.title: Combination sum
screens.prose: A classic variant: each candidate may be used **any number of times**, and order does not count. Sorting lets the loop `break` at the first candidate that is too big.
screens.question: How many lists does `combos([2, 3, 5], 8)` return?

hints.text: List sums to 8 using 2, 3 and 5, each as often as you like, in non-decreasing order.
`walk(i, ...)` passes `i`, not `i + 1`, so the same candidate can be taken again.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the sums in non-decreasing order.

byKey.orders: You counted orders: 2 + 3 + 3 and 3 + 2 + 3 are one combination. Starting the loop at `start` stops the walk going back.
byKey.no-reuse: You used each candidate once. Line 12 passes `i`, so a candidate can repeat.

explain.text: Passing `start` keeps each list non-decreasing, so each combination appears once. The `break` on line 10 prunes every larger candidate at once, because the list is sorted.

screens.title: When totals can fall
screens.question: What does `subset_sum([6, -4, 3], 2)` return?

options.why: That basket exists, but the walk never reaches it. Taking +6 makes the total 6, which passes 2, so the branch is cut before −4 is tried.
The walk is three levels deep. The bug is in which branches it cuts.
Every path ends in `return True` or `return False`.

hints.text: Follow the *take +6* branch: what is the total, and what does line 5 do?
The total is 6 here, above the target 2.
The take +6 branch is cut at once. No other basket without +6 sums to 2, so the walk returns False.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Trace the total along the *take +6* branch.

byKey.true: You found the answer by eye. The walk cut the take +6 branch at total 6, before it could add −4. That prune assumes totals only grow.

explain.text: With a negative number, a total above the target can come back down. The prune cut the only answer, 6 + (−4). A prune is safe only if a branch that fails it can never recover.

screens.title: Safe pruning
screens.prose:
Every pruned search has this shape:

```python
def search(state):
    if dead_end(state):     # can never succeed
        return
    if complete(state):
        record(state)
        return
    for choice in choices(state):
        make(choice)
        search(state)
        undo(choice)        # also after a dead end
```

The test is safe when failing it now means failing it in every extension.
screens.question: In `subset_sum` on sorted positive numbers, the walk returns `False` when `total + xs[i] > target`, without trying to skip `xs[i]`. Why is that safe?

options.text: Every later number is at least `xs[i]`, so none of them fits either
The target has already been reached
options.why: If the total equalled the target the walk would have returned True one line earlier.

options.text: Any prune is safe if the input is sorted
options.why: Sorting alone did not save the trap: with negatives, a sorted input can still dip back down.

options.text: It is not safe; it only makes the search faster
options.why: It is safe here: with numbers sorted and positive, no later number can fit if this one does not.

feedback.correct: Sorted and positive: if the smallest remaining number overshoots, every one does.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the numbers after `xs[i]` look like.

explain.text: Sorting puts the smallest remaining number at `xs[i]`. If even it overshoots, every subset of the rest overshoots too. One test then cuts the whole remaining subtree.

screens.title: Queens and targets
screens.prose: Write both searches. `n_queens(n)` returns how many safe placements of $n$ queens exist on an $n \times n$ board. `subset_sum(xs, target)` gets positive whole numbers in any order and returns whether some subset, possibly empty, sums to `target`.
screens.question: Write `n_queens(n)` and `subset_sum(xs, target)`, pruning dead ends in both.

widget.how: Check runs 13 hidden tests: queens for $n$ = 1 to 6 and 8, and subset sums with and without an answer, including an empty list. The last test has 25 even numbers and an odd target: without pruning it takes far longer than the 5-second limit.

hints.text: Queens: one row per call; skip attacked columns; undo the three sets after each recursive call.
Row minus column is the same along one diagonal, row plus column along the other.
Subset sum: return True when `total == target`; return False when `i == len(xs)` or `total + xs[i] > target`; else try take, then skip.

feedback.correct: Both searches prune and both restore their state.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 expects 2. If you got fewer, check that you remove the column and both diagonals after each recursive call.
byKey.test-5: Tests 5 expects 0 for 2 and 3 queens. Both boards have no safe placement.
byKey.test-10: Test 10 expects True: the empty subset sums to 0. Check `total == target` before anything else.
byKey.test-13: Test 13 timed out or failed. Sort first, and stop as soon as `total + xs[i]` passes the target.

explain.text: A diagonal is a fixed `row - col`, an anti-diagonal a fixed `row + col`, so three sets make every safety test $O(1)$. The sorted cut makes the last test almost instant. Two and three queens have no answers.

screens.title: Which cuts are safe
screens.prose: Three desks run backtracking searches, and each wants to prune.
screens.question: Select all that apply: which prunes are safe?

options.text: Projects costing £40k, £25k, £30k and £15k under a £70k cap: cut once spend passes £70k
Trades with exposures +£5m, −£3m, +£2m and −£4m, looking for net zero: cut once the net passes +£2m
options.why: A later short can bring the net back down: +5 − 3 + 2 − 4 = 0 passes +2 on the way.

options.text: Booking 6 analysts into 4 shifts: cut at the first analyst booked on two overlapping shifts
Picking at most 4 of those trades: cut once a fifth trade is chosen

hints.text: For each, ask whether the quantity can only grow as more choices are made.
Exposures can be negative.
Spend, clashes and the number of trades chosen never fall. Net exposure can.

feedback.correct: Spend, clashes and trade count only grow, so those cuts are safe.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A cut is safe only if the quantity cannot come back.

byKey.net: You cut on net exposure. Shorts make it fall again, so the cut can lose the answer.
byKey.rota: A clash never disappears when more analysts are booked, so cutting at the first clash is safe.

explain.text: Spend, clashes and counts are monotone: they only grow along a branch. Net exposure is not, so it is the trap again. For netting, prune on a bound instead, such as the most the remaining shorts could take off.

ideas: Pruning cuts a branch as soon as it cannot lead to an answer. It changes the work, never the answers.
A prune is safe when failing it now means failing it for every extension: spend, clashes and counts only grow.
Restore state after every branch, dead ends included. Sorting can turn one failed test into a cut of the whole rest of the loop.

quiz.prose: Three queens on a 3 by 3 board, one per row, none attacking another.
quiz.question: How many safe placements are there?

widget.label: Number of placements
widget.accept: 0: every queen in row 1 leaves row 3 with nothing safe.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Try each column for the row 1 queen.

byKey.orders: You counted $3!$ column orders. Every one puts two queens on a diagonal.
byKey.one: Check the diagonals for every start. Each one runs out of safe cells by row 3.
byKey.two: You may have checked only columns. Check both diagonals for each pair.

explain.text: A middle queen in row 1 attacks all of row 2. A corner queen leaves one cell in row 2, and that queen attacks what is left of row 3. So $n = 3$, like $n = 2$, has no answers.

quiz.prose: Without pruning, an 8-queens search puts a queen in any of the 8 columns of each row and checks the board only when it is full.
quiz.question: How many full boards does it check?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each of 8 rows has 8 choices.

byKey.perm: That is $8!$: you already ruled out repeated columns, which is a prune.
byKey.total: That counts every partial board too. Only the full boards at depth 8 are checked.

explain.text: Eight choices in each of eight rows give $8^8$ full boards. The pruned search visits only 2,057 boards in all and finds the 92 answers.

In `n_queens`, someone deletes the line that removes the column and diagonals after the recursive call.

```python

count += place(row + 1)
# cols.remove(c) ... deleted
```
quiz.question: What does `n_queens(4)` return now?

options.why: You expected the answers to survive. Without the undo, columns tried earlier stay blocked for later branches.
Leaving squares marked can only block cells. It never makes a new placement safe.
Nothing is removed any more, so no missing key can be hit.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow what `cols` holds after the first branch fails.

explain.text: The first try, r1c1, leaves column 1 and its diagonals marked forever. Later branches inherit those marks, and every answer gets blocked. Restore state after every branch, dead ends included.
